title: Local Agentic Theory For Mobile Games — Shafik Quoraishee & Joanne Song, The New York Times

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 94%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's core focus is on agent loops (perceive-predict-decide-act), planning within frame budgets, and constraint satisfaction graphs as agent harness design. The work is experimental and cross-domain, with a closing vision of billions of personalized local agents serving individuals. Working on-device demos are shown, but significant remaining needs are enumerated, placing it between applied and research. Covers constraint satisfaction, RL versus agentic AI, and 16ms frame budgets with accessible framing suitable for a mixed audience. Conference talk with live on-device demos presented at AI Engineer. Multiple direct transcript excerpts with character offsets support each key claim about agent loops, budgets, and accessibility tuning.

summary: Shafik Quoraishee and Joanne Song present experimental work from The New York Times on running agentic AI entirely on mobile devices for game playability and accessibility. They stress NYT puzzles are human-made with no AI in the actual games. The talk traces AI in games from finite state machines (Pac-Man) through reinforcement learning (AlphaGo, AlphaZero, EfficientZero) to agentic systems that reason over game state using on-device language models via an agentic loop with tool calls and in-context learning. Demos include a Space Invaders agent and a mini crossword solver using a constraint satisfaction graph with backtracking. The central engineering challenge is fitting agent planning within a 16-millisecond frame budget across space, time, and energy constraints on mobile hardware. Joanne then reframes accessibility: traditional games use fixed state models with static toggles, but WCAG 2.2 provides a proven framework across perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust pillars, and WCAG 3.0 is moving toward graded bronze/silver/gold scoring rather than binary pass/fail. The talk argues accessibility and difficulty should stop being separate toggles and become two ends of one dial the agent tunes to the player in real time. On-device vision models track eye gaze to detect search friction, analyze shaky taps for control difficulty, support handwriting recognition, monitor focus paths to flag keyboard traps and inject exit routes, and act as a live layout auditor that dynamically resizes controls. Remaining needs include faster 16ms planning, predictive models for layout changes, long-term personal memory, a shared game state language across titles, better chips, and honest benchmarks. The closing bet is that the future of AI is billions of small local brains, each shaped by the person it serves.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: NYT puzzles are made by people with no AI in the games; this work is experimental and focused on playability and accessibility, not game generation.
On-device agentic AI eliminates cloud round-trip latency, preserves privacy, works offline, and enables deep personalization.
Reinforcement learning changes model weights through training; agentic systems use language models with in-context learning to reason over game state through an agentic loop with no reward system.
The on-device budget has three axes—space, time (16ms per 60Hz frame), and energy (battery)—managed via a constraint graph with soft and hard penalties, penalizing time overruns most.

Accessibility should move from binary toggles to graded dials an agent tunes in real time, grounded in WCAG 2.2 pillars (perceivable, operable, understandable, robust) and WCAG 3.0's bronze/silver/gold trend.
An on-device agent can sense eye gaze, shaky taps, and focus traps, then act by injecting exit routes and dynamically resizing controls.
Accessibility and difficulty are two ends of one dial the agent constantly tunes to the player's live context, not separate menus.
Remaining needs include faster 16ms planning, predictive layout models, long-term personal memory, a shared game state language, better chips, and honest benchmarks.
The future of AI is billions of small local brains, each shaped entirely by the individual it serves, rather than one giant centralized cloud brain.
Understand the distinction between RL-based game AI (weight changes via training) and agentic game AI (in-context reasoning via language models).

sections.title: Disclaimers and experimental framing
sections.summary: Speakers clarify NYT puzzles are human-made, AI-free, and that the work is experimental—exploring agent capabilities for solvability, playability, and other on-device features rather than game generation. References a prior World Fair talk on connections solvers.

sections.title: A short history of AI in games
sections.summary: Traces AI in games from 1980s finite state machines (Pac-Man ghosts) through RL milestones (AlphaGo, AlphaZero, EfficientZero V2), establishing the lineage leading to agentic systems.

sections.title: Why run the AI on the device, not the cloud
sections.summary: Argues for on-device AI: lower latency (no cloud round-trip), privacy (computation stays local), offline capability (subway tunnels), and personalization. Cloud architecture is expensive and introduces latency for mobile apps.

sections.title: From reinforcement learning to agentic play
sections.summary: Distinguishes RL (changes model weights through training cycles, reward systems) from agentic systems (language models reason over game state via in-context learning, tool calls, agentic loop, no reward to grind—more dynamic and adaptive).

sections.title: Demo: Space Invaders agent
sections.summary: Shows an on-device agentic Space Invaders player with a perceive-predict-decide-act loop, displaying the agent's internal states on the right side of the screen.

sections.title: The on-device budget: space, time, and energy
sections.summary: Details three budget axes: space (weights, compressed state history, planning artifacts, render headroom), time (16ms per 60Hz frame—exceeding causes jank), energy (battery; NPUs emerging but not sufficient). A constraint graph balances these with soft and hard penalties, penalizing time overruns most. Gaze estimation via CNNs adds an input modality. Arc AGI score indicates base model intelligence is not yet sufficient.

sections.title: Demo: mini crossword solver and generalist models
sections.summary: Demonstrates a constraint satisfaction agent solving the NYT mini crossword using a backtracking graph that retreats when constraints become crowded or incorrect, using natural language from the graph. Closes by mentioning generalist models like Google Seema as candidates for the agentic framework.

sections.title: Accessibility: from toggles to graded dials
sections.summary: Joanne grounds accessibility design in WCAG 2.2's four pillars (perceivable, operable, understandable, robust) and notes WCAG 3.0's move to graded bronze/silver/gold scoring. Static easy modes can't fix grids blind to real-time needs. Core dials—input tolerance and step granularity—scale with player needs, and the agent dynamically calculates them against live context.

sections.title: The agent tuning the game to you in real time
sections.summary: On-device vision models track eye gaze for search friction, analyze shaky taps, support handwriting recognition, and detect focus traps in broken dialogues—injecting exit routes live. The agent acts as a live layout auditor, dynamically resizing controls. Accessibility and difficulty become two ends of one dial in a real-time tug-of-war between system and player.

sections.title: What is still needed, and billions of local brains
sections.summary: Lists remaining groundwork: faster 16ms planning, predictive layout models, long-term personal memory, a shared game state language across games, better chips, and honest benchmarks. Closing bet: the future of AI is billions of small local brains, each shaped by the individual it serves, not one giant centralized brain.

demonstrations: An on-device agentic Space Invaders player that perceives the scene, predicts alien moves, decides actions, and loops within the frame budget.
A constraint satisfaction agent solving the NYT mini crossword using a backtracking graph that retreats when fills stop fitting.
An agent detecting a broken dialogue keyboard trap, flagging the focus loop, and injecting an exit route live on device.
An agent acting as a live layout auditor that measures the interface, catches violations, and dynamically resizes controls for limited dexterity.
limitations: Mobile devices are not yet optimized for agentic workloads; battery drains fast without careful energy management.
Base model intelligence is insufficient for fully cognizant decisions in the most complex and interesting future games.
Agent loop design must be heavily curated to minimize energy processing on current hardware.
Local agents still need faster 16ms planning, predictive layout models, long-term personal memory, a shared game state language, better chips, and honest benchmarks to truly understand games.
quantitativeClaims: At 60Hz refresh rate, each frame is 16 milliseconds, and agent planning must fit within that window or jank occurs.
EfficientZero and EfficientZero V2 are described as sample-efficient RL models that learn with far less data than traditional RL.
WCAG 3.0 is moving from binary pass/fail to graded bronze, silver, and gold scoring.
